title: The Rajasuya Completed
story:
The great fire that had burned for the Rajasuya was at last allowed to grow quiet.

Months had passed since the tribute of the four quarters had poured into Indraprastha, since the kings of the earth had gathered in the hall, since the first honor had been given and the storm around it weathered. The sacrifice had been fed with offerings day after day, its rites performed by the priests in their appointed order, its splendor witnessed by gods and men alike. A rite of that scale does not close itself; it has to be carried through to its end by someone whose will can hold it there, and the chronicle is plain about whose will that was. And through it all, it was Krishna — the lord of the lords of yoga, as the chronicle names him — who completed the great rite for the king.

When the final oblations were done, Krishna bestowed the fees of the sacrifice: ample gifts, given without stint, to the officiating priests and to all who had sat in the assembly. The gifts were as generous as the rite itself had been, measured out to every priest who had served the fire and every learned man who had kept the assembly company. No one who had served the rite went away empty-handed. Then came the avabhritha, the concluding bath, and Yudhishthira stepped down into the water and was cleansed — the emperor washed clean of the great rite, the Rajasuya finished and its fruit secured. The emperor came out of the water an emperor; the rite had done what rites are for, and the kingdom had its crowning.

Yet Krishna did not leave. He stayed on in Indraprastha, month after month, as a friend stays past the hour of his departure because the house does not want him to go. They were quiet months after the great noise of the rite — the city still full of its guests, the king still warm from the honour that had crowned him, and Krishna among them not as a visiting lord but as one of the household. And when at last he asked leave of the king, Yudhishthira was reluctant to give it, and could hardly bear the asking. But Krishna took leave all the same, and turned his face toward his own city, and the road to Dwaraka received him.

Then the guests departed, and Indraprastha began to empty. Gods and men and the beings of the air, every one of them honored by the king as they went, carried away from that city nothing but praise — praise of Krishna, and praise of the sacrifice he had completed, and the memory of a rite that had crowned a king of the earth. They left with the king's honours on them and good words in their mouths; a feast of that size is meant to be remembered, and this one was, by everyone who had shared it.

Almost every one of them.

One guest of the Kurus left Indraprastha in a different temper entirely. Duryodhana, the wicked one — the strife itself, the disease of the Kuru line, as the tellers of the tale name him — could not endure the Pandavas' prosperity. Where the other guests carried praise home, he carried the sight of their splendor like a coal pressed to the palm, and the pain of it did not cool on the road. He came to it grudging and left it burning, and what stayed with him was the fact of their greatness itself — a fact he would spend the coming months trying to undo.

The fires of the Rajasuya were out. The treasury stood full, the emperor was crowned, the guests had scattered to their kingdoms. Only that one burning grievance remained, traveling back to Hastinapura in the heart of a prince who had shared in none of the joy — and it arrived there before any of the praise did.
reflection: The Rajasuya ends in harmony, leave-taking, and praise — and the only discord is carried out by a guest who took no part in any of it. Duryodhana's envy does not touch the sacrifice itself, but it plants a wound in him that the coming months will only deepen.
next_story_tease: The grievance Duryodhana carried out of Indraprastha would find its wound soon after, in the mirrored hall that Maya had built.
hero_scene: The guests of the Rajasuya stream out of Indraprastha in the evening light, praising Krishna as he turns his chariot toward Dwaraka — while Duryodhana rides apart, alone, his face dark as he looks back at the city's splendor.
